title: TypedDict + TypeGuard order validation
prompt:
Build the typed order model:

1. `Status = Literal['pending', 'paid', 'shipped']`
2. `class Order(TypedDict, total=False)` with fields `id: int`, `status: Status`, `items: List[str]`, `note: Optional[str]`
3. `is_valid_order(data) -> TypeGuard[Order]` returning True only when: data is a dict; `id` is a true int (bool rejected); `status` is one of the three literals; `items` is a list of str
4. `status_of(order) -> Status` returning the status field

Be strict about bool: in Python `isinstance(True, int)` is True, so a bare isinstance check accepts booleans — reject them.
boilerplate:
from typing import TypedDict, Literal, TypeGuard, List, Optional

# TODO: Status, Order, is_valid_order, status_of

tests.name: valid orders pass, garbage fails
tests.code:
good = {'id': 7, 'status': 'paid', 'items': ['a', 'b']}
assert is_valid_order(good)
assert status_of(good) == 'paid'
for bad in (
    {'id': True, 'status': 'paid', 'items': []},
    {'id': 1, 'status': 'returned', 'items': []},
    {'id': 1, 'status': 'paid', 'items': 'ab'},
    {'id': 1, 'status': 'paid'},
    'nope',
    42,
):
    assert not is_valid_order(bad), f'must reject: {bad!r}'
print('ok')
tests.hint: Check dict-ness, true-int id (reject bool), literal status membership, and list-of-str items.

tests.name: bool rejection is explicit
tests.code:
assert is_valid_order({'id': 0, 'status': 'pending', 'items': []})
assert not is_valid_order({'id': False, 'status': 'pending', 'items': []})
print('ok')
tests.hint: id 0 is valid; False is not — the bool check must be explicit.
